name: La Laguna
why: A roomy Third Street taqueria whose carnitas, soft with crisped edges, are the reason to cross town. Daytime only.
story: A plain, spacious taqueria on Third Street serving the standard run of tacos, huevos rancheros and big lunch plates. The pork is the point: carnitas slow-cooked until soft and crisped at the edges, best packed into a super burrito. There are plenty of tables, which is rare for a taqueria this good.
practical: Weekdays 9 am to 4 pm; Saturday 10 am to 2 pm (listing)
hours: Mon to Fri 9 am to 4 pm; Sat 10 am to 2 pm (listing, confirm)
flags: Single editorial source (Infatuation Bayview guide, updated 2025).
A search summary credits owner Renato Ray Guerrero for the carnitas and horchata; source unknown, left out.
Hours are daytime only, so evening was dropped.
Hours from listing sites.

name: The Boys' Deli
kind: Deli counter inside a family market
why: A sandwich counter at the back of a Polk Street produce market, started by two cousins who grew up in their uncle's pizza shop. Big, Boar's Head-based sandwiches at fair prices.
story: Two cousins started this counter in the early 2000s inside their family's Polk and Green produce market. They knew pizza, not sandwiches, until the day their Uncle Joe pulled a hot sandwich out of his pizza oven. Now the board runs from an Italian sub to the house Sanfranpsycho: honey turkey, gouda, pesto and remoulade.
practical: Inside Polk and Green Produce Market
hours: Mon to Sat 9 am to 8 pm; Sun 9 am to 6 pm (listing, confirm)
flags: Origin story is from the deli's own site; no editorial source fetched.
SFGate Russian Hill roundup (candidate source) disallows fetching; not used.
Two locations (Polk St, San Bruno).

name: Escape From New York Pizza
why: The original Haight Street slice counter from 1986, co-founded by one of Amoeba's founders and now owned partly by staff who started at the bottom. Open past 1 a.m. on weekends.
story: Paul Geffner and Joe Goldmark, also a founding owner of Amoeba Records, opened this Haight Street slice shop in October 1986. It grew to five shops and has since shrunk back to two. Most of the owners worked their way up from the counter, one from handing out flyers at Haight and Clayton.
order: A New York-style slice off the counter, whatever came out last.
practical: Pickup until 1:30 am Fri and Sat
hours: Pickup Mon to Wed 10:30 am to 9:30 pm; Thu to 10:30 pm; Fri and Sat to 1:30 am; Sun to 9:30 pm (own site)
flags: Ownership details are from 2016 (Hoodline); confirm.
Fillmore posters, rock autographs and a Matt Groening drawing on the walls come from search summaries; left out of the story.
Now two locations (Haight St and Bush St), so not a chain by the rule.

name: Shan Dong
kind: Shandong noodle and dumpling house, since 1991
why: A 1991 family restaurant pulling thick noodles behind a glass counter, run by the son who left college to help his parents. Oakland Chinatown's busiest room.
story: Helen and Brang Hung came from Taiwan in 1982, washing dishes and nannying until they opened Shan Dong in 1991, where Brang cooked the food of his home province. Six months in, their son Charles left City College to help and never left. The thick noodles are still pulled by hand behind glass at the front.
order: Sesame paste noodles, Shan Dong dumplings and dry-braised green beans.
practical: Closes for an hour between lunch and dinner
flags: Family history is from East Bay Express (2017); confirm Charles Hung still runs it.
Brang Hung's dishwashing job is described in the article; kept as context.
Hours not confirmed.

name: Dan Sung Sa
why: A dark Korean drinking house with wooden booths and old movie posters that stays open well past most of Oakland. Galbi, kimchi fried rice and soju until late.
story: A dark, loud Korean pub on Telegraph that stays open past 1 a.m., long after most of Oakland has closed. Racy posters and magazine pages long earned it a cheeky nickname among regulars. The food is drinking food: kimchi fried rice, barbecued galbi and chicken wings, alongside plenty of soju.
order: BBQ galbi and kimchi fried rice with a bottle of soju.
flags: Infatuation review says open until 1 am in the body and 2 am in the summary; confirm.
Its regulars' nickname is crude; kept out of the story on purpose. Dan to decide whether to mention it.
Wooden soju-room booths come from a search summary; confirm on a visit.
Area set to Northgate per the review; candidate said Uptown.

name: Los Mexicanos Bakery
why: A low-key Fruitvale panadería open at 5 a.m., cash only, with a parking lot and seasonal breads like rosca de reyes. Old-school but little written about it.
story: A small Fruitvale bakery and sandwich counter with cases of pan dulce and cakes made to order for birthdays and weddings. It opens at 5 a.m. most days, takes cash only and has its own parking lot. In January it bakes rosca de reyes, and pan de muerto comes out for Día de Muertos.
order: A concha or two, and rosca de reyes if it is January.
hours: Mon to Fri 5 am to 6 pm; Sat 5 am to 5 pm; Sun 6 am to 4 pm (listing, confirm)
flags: Community/listing sources only.
Oaklandside (2021) calls it an Oakland mainstay since the 1980s; disallowed for fetching, so the year is left out.
The listing says pan de muerto comes out in March, which contradicts Día de Muertos (November); used the holiday only.
A Los Mexicanos Bakery No. 2 exists; confirm which shop this is.

name: Champa Garden
why: A family Lao-Thai room in a former doughnut shop, known for its rice-ball salad. One of the few Lao kitchens in Oakland with a following.
story: In 2006 Phuoc Nguyen, his wife and his father-in-law turned an old East Oakland doughnut shop into Champa Garden, cooking Lao, Thai and what he calls Californian food. The draw is the rice-ball salad: crisp rice, cured pork, peanuts and herbs wrapped in lettuce. A 2013 San Francisco branch followed.
practical: Second location on Ocean Ave in San Francisco
flags: Tasting Table piece is from 2013; confirm the family still runs it.
LocalWiki would not load (HTTP 522); listed from search results only.
Hours not confirmed.

name: Fentons Creamery
why: California's longest continuously running creamery, the claimed birthplace of rocky road, and the parlor Pixar wrote into Up. Busy, but a true Oakland institution.
story: Eldridge Seth Fenton opened his creamery in 1894 at 41st and Howe, and it moved a few blocks to Piedmont Avenue in 1961. The family credits a grandson, Melvin Fenton, with creating rocky road. After a 2001 fire it was rebuilt bigger, and Pixar regulars later put it into Up.
order: A scoop of rocky road, or a sundae to share.
practical: Grill menu as well as ice cream
flags: Wikipedia dates Melvin Fenton's rocky road to 1894, which conflicts with him being the founder's grandson; story avoids a year.
Candidate listed late; no late hours found, dropped. Hours not confirmed.
Disney Food Blog not fetched.

name: Asmara Restaurant
why: The East Bay's oldest continuously running Eritrean and Ethiopian restaurant, opened in 1985 by a couple who still own the building. Their sons have stepped in.
story: Kesete and Okba Yohannes opened Asmara on Telegraph in October 1985; it was Okba's idea, since her family had run a restaurant in Zalambessa on the Ethiopia-Eritrea border. Buying the building early helped it outlast most of the block. Their sons Benyam and Yonathan have since taken a larger role.
order: A mix of stews on injera to share.
flags: East Bay Express article is from 2017; confirm current management.
Menu page would not render; order line is general, not from a source.
SF Chronicle (2023) also profiled it; disallowed for fetching.
Hours not confirmed.

name: Oceanview Diner
why: The old Bette's on Fourth Street, saved in 2022 by seven of its own staff, who kept the jukebox, the decor and the recipes. Now on its way to full worker ownership.
story: Bette and Manfred Kroening opened Bette's in 1982 as Fourth Street was taking shape. When Manfred retired in January 2022, seven longtime staff, including the chef of nearly four decades, bought the recipes, kept the jukebox and retro decor, and reopened that March as Oceanview Diner, set up to become fully worker-owned.
order: Buttermilk pancakes, or scrapple with eggs.
flags: Berkeleyside disallows fetching; the March 2022 reopening date comes from its headline and search summary.
Worker-ownership status after 2022 not confirmed (the plan was to pay off the landlord's loan first).
Hours not confirmed.

name: Funky Elephant
why: A roughly 15-seat Thai counter in a West Berkeley strip mall, run by a former Hawker Fare chef, with curry pastes made in house and a Michelin Guide listing.
story: Supasit Puttikaew left his job as chef de cuisine at Hawker Fare in San Francisco to open this small counter with Nanchaphon Laptanachai around the end of 2017. They pound their own curry pastes and cook bold Thai comfort food in a strip-mall room with a dog-friendly patio, including their own take on khao man gai.
order: Khao man gai, and the chili-jam wings if they are on.
practical: Afternoon break between lunch and dinner
hours: Tue to Fri 11:30 am to 2:30 pm and 5 to 8:30 pm; Sat and Sun noon to 3 pm and 5 to 8:30 pm (own site)
flags: Opening date inferred from press excerpts on the restaurant's site (Nov 2017, Jan 2018).
Seat count, patio and chili-jam wings come from search summaries.
Michelin Guide mention is from the restaurant's own site.

name: Ole's Waffle Shop
why: A Park Street waffle diner from 1927, owned by one family since the 1960s, with a restored neon sign. Its best-known waitress served nearly 50 years.
story: Open since 1927, Ole's once had an Oakland branch too; that site is now a parking lot. One family has owned it since the 1960s, and a facade remodel restored its 60-year-old neon sign. Waitress Dolores Jeanpierre served there for nearly half a century; customers lined up outside to see her off in 2021.
order: A waffle, made from the house batter.
flags: Founder Ole Swanson and the original-batter claim come from a search summary of an unofficial site; left out.
Preservation society piece dates from about 2013 (86th year).
Hours not confirmed.

name: The Bread Basket
why: A 1977 Filipino bakery at the top of Mission Street that three cousins took over in 2025 when their aunt retired. Pandesal, ensaymada and bibingka from family recipes.
story: Auntie Nelly and Uncle Sonny opened the bakery in 1977 with recipes from the Philippines. When Nelly retired in 2025, three nephews took over: they grew up working the family bakery in Guam, then became a Marine and photographer, a contractor, and a baker who ran the family's Modesto shop. The pandesal still comes out early.
order: A bag of warm pandesal and an ensaymada.
flags: History is from the bakery's own About page.
Palo Alto Online crawl (Dec 2023) not fetched; oven times of 5 am and pastries at 7 to 9 am come from its search summary.
Related family bakeries in Guam and Modesto; this is the only Bay Area one found.
Hours not confirmed.

name: Duc Huong Sandwiches
why: A Little Saigon bánh mì shop whose crisp, chewy baguettes 7x7 ranks close to the best outside Vietnam. Little is published about its history.
story: A plain counter on Story Road selling bánh mì on baguettes that shatter outside and stay soft and chewy within, with a long list of fillings. It has a second shop on McKee Road. Regulars treat the đặc biệt, the house combination of cold cuts, as the default order.
flags: Single editorial source (7x7, updated Oct 2025).
Đặc biệt as the regular order comes from listing-site summaries.
Hours not confirmed.

name: La Palma Mexicatessen
why: A 1953 grocery, tortilla factory and kitchen on 24th Street, billed as the Mission's longest-running Latino-owned business. Masa ground daily from nixtamal.
story: Part grocery, part tortilla factory and part kitchen, La Palma has stood at 24th and Florida since 1953 and calls itself the Mission's longest-running Latino-owned business. The Castaño Ibarra family bought it in 1983. Masa is made daily from nixtamal for tortillas, sopes and tamales, and the holiday tamale line runs out the door.
order: A dozen tamales, or carnitas with fresh handmade tortillas.
practical: Grocery, tortillería and hot food under one roof
Long tamale lines at the holidays
flags: 1983 purchase and the nixtamal process come from a search summary of the shop's own site.
SF Foghorn page did not render; listed from search results.
